transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess I’m here because after these nights where I eat like that, I just sit there with crumbs and empty containers all around me, and I feel so ashamed. Disgusted with myself, really. And then the next morning I can hardly pray, or look folks at church in the eye. It’s gotten to where I just thought… I can’t keep doing this by myself.
How often do these episodes happen, and are they usually triggered by something specific, like stress or being alone?

Since my friend passed, that’s when it really started being… regular, I suppose. Mostly late at night. It happens at least once or twice most weeks, and honestly, I can’t think of a month where it’s truly let up.

I mean, grief does funny things to a person. We used to talk on the phone in the evenings, you know, and now the house just feels so quiet then. But yes… it’s been most weeks.
After these episodes of overeating, do you ever try to compensate by making yourself sick, exercising a lot, or using laxatives or diet pills?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly… when you say “compensate,” do you mean like doing something on purpose right after? Because mostly I just feel awful and sort of… sit with it, and then I try to clean things up before morning.

I don’t really keep track of those kinds of things. My mind goes to, “Lord, why did I do this again,” and then I start thinking about what people would think if they knew… I’m sorry, I know I’m wandering. I guess I’m not sure what all would count.
During these episodes, do you ever feel like you can’t stop eating or control what you’re eating, even if you wanted to?

Yes… yes, that’s exactly how it feels. Once I take that first bite after the house has gone quiet, it’s like my good sense just steps aside somewhere. I’ll be sitting there telling myself, “Belinda, stop now, you don’t need any more,” but my hands just keep reaching.

And it’s strange, because in the daytime I can be reasonable about things, you know, make lists, keep the kitchen tidy, remember who needs a casserole at church… but at night, in that moment, it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing the way I ought to be choosing. I want to stop, and then I don’t. Or I can’t. It shames me to say it.
Do these episodes interfere with your daily life, like making it hard to focus on work, go to church, or spend time with family?

Yes… I suppose it does, more than I’d like to admit. I’ve started saying no to some bridge nights, and I’ve backed out of helping with the church kitchen a few times.

It’s silly, maybe, but I get so worried someone will notice leftovers are missing, or that they’ll look at me and somehow know I’m ashamed. And then I make excuses—say I’m tired, or I’ve got things to do at home. Which, I mean, there’s always something at home, isn’t there? Laundry doesn’t fold itself. But really, sometimes I’m just avoiding people.
Do these episodes ever make it hard for you to participate in certain activities or connect with people, even outside of church or family gatherings, like at work or in your community?

Yes… I mean, I’m not working now, so it’s not work exactly, but it does make me pull back. I’ll turn down bridge nights sometimes, and I’ve stopped helping with the church kitchen here and there.

It’s that worry that someone will notice things—leftovers missing, or just look at me and see that I’m ashamed. And then I start making excuses. Funny, I used to always bring the lemon squares for bridge… well, not funny, I guess. I just don’t want people asking questions.
Do these eating episodes cause you a lot of emotional distress, or make it harder for you to feel comfortable around other people, even when food isn’t involved?

Yes… that’s really why I came, I think. After one of those nights, I’ll just sit there with crumbs on my nightgown and empty containers around me, and I feel so ashamed—just disgusted with myself.

And then the next morning, even if food isn’t anywhere involved, I can hardly look people in the eye at church. I’ll try to pray, and my mind just goes right back to what I did, and I feel like… like I’m not the woman everybody thinks I am. It makes it hard to be around folks, yes.
Do you usually eat during these episodes even when you’re not really hungry, or does it typically start because you’re feeling physically hungry?

I’m not sure I can say cleanly. Sometimes I think I’m hungry, but then I wonder if I’m just… restless, or upset, or I’ve got that empty sort of feeling that isn’t exactly stomach hunger.

It’s hard to tell the difference once it starts. I’ll think, “Well, I didn’t have much for supper,” but then—oh, I don’t know. My mother used to always say you should never grocery shop on an empty stomach, and I suppose that’s true, though I’m not usually out shopping when it happens. I’m usually just at home, and then it sort of gets away from me.

So… I guess I haven’t really noticed whether it always starts from being truly hungry. I’m not sure.
During these episodes, do you find yourself eating much more quickly than usual, like finishing food before you even realize how fast you've eaten it?

Yes… yes, I do. I’ll be standing right there at the kitchen counter, and it’s like I’m not even properly eating. I’ll have pound cake, or crackers, and before I know it I’ve gone through so much of it I barely tasted it.

Sometimes I catch myself swallowing before I’ve really chewed it right, which sounds awful to say out loud. My mother would’ve had a fit about that—she was always after us to sit at the table and eat like civilized people. But in those moments I’m just… rushing, like I have to get it down before I can think about it.
Do you usually eat during these episodes by yourself, and if so, is it because you're uncomfortable eating in front of others or worry they might notice something?

Yes… I do. Especially if it’s something like bridge night, or a church supper. I’ll make sure people see me with just a modest little plate, you know, nothing that would make anyone look twice.

And then later, when everyone’s gone home and things are quiet, I’ll go back into the kitchen and pull out the leftovers. I’ll eat standing there where nobody can see me. It’s embarrassing to admit that. I suppose I’m afraid somebody would notice how much I really want, or… what I’m like when I’m not trying to look proper.
